stem_md: Let  $ABC$  be a triangle with circumscribed and inscribed circles  $(O)$  and  $(I)$  respectively.  $AA'$ , $BB'$ , $CC'$  are the bisectors of triangle  $ABC$ . Prove that  $OI$  passes through the the isogonal conjugate of  point   $I$  with respect to triangle   $A'B'C'$ .
solution_md:
Solved with **MathsCrazy** and a few other for a while (he suggested the Pedal triangle idea) and also with help of **Siddharth03** (he told me that  $OI$  is the Euler line of the intouch triangle)

Note that  $OI$  is the Euler line of the intouch triangle, say  $\triangle DEF$ . Then, note that midpoint of  $OI'$  where  $I'$  is the isogonal conjugate of  $I'$   in  $\triangle A'B'C'$ , is the centre of the Pedal triangle of  $I$  in  $A'B'C'$ . We now invert about  $I$ . Then,  $A$ ,  $B$ ,  $C$  become midpoints of  $EF$ ,  $FD$ ,  $DE$  respectively. Now,  $I$  being circumcentre of  $DEF$  becomes orthocentre of  $ABC$ . Now,  $I$ ,  $A$  and  $A'$  are collinear and so are  $B$ ,  $A'$ ,  $C$  so,  $I$ ,  $A$ ,  $A'$  are still colinear and  $A'$  lies on  $(IBC)$ . infact,  $(IBC)$  also passes through  $D$ . So infact,  $A'$ ,  $B'$  and  $C'$  are reflections about  $BC$ ,  $CA$  and  $AB$  of  $A$ ,  $B$ , and  $C$  respectively. Now, feet from  $I$  onto  $A'B'$  becomes diametrically opposite point to  $I$  in  $(IA'B')$ . Further, the line connecting  $I$  to the centre of the pedal triangle is same as that connecting  $I$  to centre of the inverted pedal triangle. Take a homotethy of factor  $\frac{1}{2}$  at  $I$ , thus we get the centre of triangle formed by circumcentres of  $(IA'B')$ ,  $(IB'C')$  and  $(IC'A')$ . These are formed by the perpendicular bisectors of  $IA'$ ,  $IB'$  and  $IC'$ . Since  $BC$ ,  $CA$  and  $AB$  are perpendicular bisectors of  $AA'$ ,  $BB'$ ,  $CC'$ , we have that the distances of the perpendicular bisectors of  $IA'$ ,  $IB'$  and  $IC'$  from  $BC$ ,  $CA$  and  $AB$  are  $\frac{IA}{2}$ ,  $\frac{IB}{2}$ ,  $\frac{IC}{2}$ , which are also the distances of the circumcentre of  $ABC$  from its sides. Thus the circumcentre of  $(ABC)$  is the homotethy centre of  $(ABC)$  and the inverted homotethic Pedal triangle, thus is centre of the homotethic Pedal triangle, and we are done.

stem_md:
Given triangle  $ABC$  and  $P,Q$  are two isogonal conjugate points in  $\triangle ABC$ .  $AP,AQ$  intersects  $(QBC)$  and  $(PBC)$  at  $M,N$ , respectively (  $M,N$  be inside triangle  $ABC$ )
1. Prove that  $M,N,P,Q$  locate on a circle - named  $(I)$ 2.   $MN\cap PQ$  at  $J$ . Prove that  $IJ$  passed through a fixed line when  $P,Q$  changed
solution_md: $AP$  cuts  $\odot(PBC)$  and  $\odot(QBC)$  again at  $Q',N',$  respectively and  $AQ$  cuts  $\odot(PBC)$  and  $\odot(QBC)$  again at  $M',P',$  respectively. It's known that the inversion with center  $A$  and power  $AB \cdot AC$  followed by the symmetry on the angle bisector of  $\angle BAC$  swaps  $\odot(PBC)$  and  $\odot(QBC),$  thus this swaps  $\{P,P'\},$   $\{Q,Q'\}$   $\{M,M'\},$   $\{N,N'\}$   $\Longrightarrow$   $AP \cdot AP'=AN \cdot AN'$   $\Longrightarrow$   $PN \parallel P'N',$  thus by Reim's theorem, it follows that  $P',Q',M',N'$  are concyclic  $\Longrightarrow$   $P,Q,M,N$  are concyclic. $PN,MQ,BC$  are pairwise radical axes of  $\odot(ABC),$   $\odot(PBC)$  and  $\odot(QBC),$  concurring at their radical center  $R.$  Thus if  $AR$  cuts  $\odot(ABC)$  again at  $X,$  we have  $RX \cdot RA=RB \cdot RC=RP \cdot RN$   $\Longrightarrow$   $X \in \odot(APN)$   $\Longrightarrow$   $X$  is the Miquel point of the complete cyclic  $PMQN$   $\Longrightarrow$   $I,J,X$  are collinear and  $\overline{IJX} \perp AR$  (well-known), i.e.  $\angle AXI=90^{\circ}$   $\Longrightarrow$   $IJ$  passes through the antipode of  $A$  on  $\odot(ABC),$  obviously fixed.

stem_md: Find all positive integers  $a,b,c$  satisfying  $(a,b)=(b,c)=(c,a)=1$  and \[ \begin{cases} a^2+b\mid b^2+c b^2+c\mid c^2+a \end{cases} \] and none of prime divisors of  $a^2+b$  are congruent to  $1$  modulo  $7$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Link</summary>http://diendantoanhoc.net/topic/151166-s%E1%BB%91-h%E1%BB%8Dc-thpt-th%C3%A1ng-11-t%C3%ACm-abc-tho%E1%BA%A3-a2b-mid-b2c-b2c-mid-c2a/</details>
That is my solution. I will translate to English.  $$ \begin{cases} (a^{2} + b)\mid (c^{2} + a)  (a^{2} + b)\mid (b^{4} - c^{2}) \end{cases} \implies (a^{2} + b)\mid (b^{4} + a) \implies (a^{2} + b)\mid (b^{8} - a^{2}) \implies (a^{2} + b)\mid ((b^{8} - a^{16}) + (a^{16} - a^{2}) \implies (a^{2} + b)\mid a^{2}(a^{14} - 1) $$  Note that  $\text{gcd}(a^{2} + b; a^{2})\mid \text{gcd}(b; a^{2})\mid \text{gcd}(a^{2}; b^{2})\mid (\text{gcd}(a; b))^{2} = 1 \implies \text{gcd}(a^{2} + b; a^{2}) = 1$   $$ \implies (a^{2} + b)\mid (a^{14} - 1) $$  Denote  $p$  is a prime factor of  $a^{2} + b$ Case 1.  $p = 7$ . Obviously,  $\text{gcd}(p; a) = 1$ , by Fermat Little's theorem:  $1 \equiv a^{14} \equiv a^{2} \pmod{7}$ . Therefore  $7\mid (a^{2} - 1)$ . By LTE's lemma  $v_{7}(a^{14} - 1) = v_{7}(a^{2} - 1) + 1$ . Hence,  $v_{7}(a^{2} + b) \le v_{7}(7(a^{2} - 1))$ Case 2.  $p \neq 7$ . If  $p\mid \frac{a^{14} - 1}{a^{2} - 1}$ , by an old, well-known lemma: "Let  $L, x$  be positive integers and  $p$  be a prime number such that  $L\mid \frac{x^{p} - 1}{x - 1}$  then  $L \equiv 0; 1 \pmod{p}$ ". Which means  $p \equiv 0; 1\pmod{7}$ , contradition. Thus, all prime factors  $q \not\equiv 0; 1\pmod{7}$  of  $a^{2} + b$  is also the prime factor  $a^{2} - 1$ Hence, we conclude  $(a^{2} + b) \mid 7(a^{2} - 1)$ . Setting  $7(a^{2} - 1) = L(a^{2} + b) \iff (7 - L)(a^{2} + b) = 7(b + 1)$ . Hence,  $L \ge 6$  $a^{2} + b = \frac{7(1 + b)}{7 - L} \implies \frac{7(1 + b)}{7 - L}\mid 7(b^{2} - 1) + 7(c + 1) \implies \frac{7(b + 1)}{7 - L}\mid 7(c + 1) \implies \frac{7(b + 1)}{7 - L}\mid 7(c^{2} - 1) + 7(1 + a) \implies \frac{7(b + 1)}{7 - L} \mid 7(a + 1)$ . Therefore,  $$ \frac{7(a + 1)}{a^{2} + b} \in \mathbb{Z}_{+} $$  .
Try  $a$  from  $1$  to  $8$  we get  $(1; 1; 1); (6; 13; 370)$  are solutions. Because  $a, b, c$  are pairwise prime. So  $(1; 1; 1)$  is the unique solution.

stem_md: Find all integes  $a,b,c,d$  that form an arithmetic progression satisfying  $d-c+1$  is prime number and  $a+b^2+c^3=d^2b$
solution_md:
Let  $k$  be the common difference in the aritmetic progression which contains the consecutive terms  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$  and  $d$ .  Hence  $a=b-k$ ,  $c=b+k$  and  $d=b+2k$ , which inserted in the equation $(1) \;\; a + b^2 + c^3 = d^2b$ result in $(b - k) + b^2 + (b+k)^3 = (b+2k)^2b$ ,

i.e. $(k-1)[b^2 + (k+1)b - k(k+1)] = 0$ .

Hence we have  $k=1$  or  $(2) \;\; b^2 + (k+1)b - k(k+1) = 0$ .

Applying the fact that  $d - c + 1 = k + 1 = p$  is a prime combined with equation (2) (which after replacing  $k$  with  $p-1$  becomes) $(3) \;\; b^2 + pb - p(p-1) = 0$ we obtain  $p|b^2$ .  Therefore  $p|b$  (since  $p$  is a prime), i.e. there is an integer  $x$  s.t.  $b=px$ , which inserted in (3) give us ${\textstyle (4) \;\; x^2 + x - 1 = - \frac{1}{p}}$ .

Equation (4) has obviously no integer solution  $x$  (since  $p \in \mathbb{P}$  implies  ${\textstyle \frac{1}{p} \not \in \mathbb{Z}}$ ).**Conclusion:**  Under the given condition equations (1) is solvable iff  $k=1$ , i.e.  $(a,b,c,d) = (n,n+1,n+2,n+3)$ , where  $n$  is an arbitrary integer.

stem_md: Find all triples of integers  $(a, b, c)$  satisfying  $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 =3(ab + bc + ca).$
solution_md:
First we will prove  $(a,b,c)=(0,0,0)$ . 
Let  $gcd(a,b,c)=d$   Let   $a=dx$    $ b=dy $   $c=dz$  . $x^2+y^2+z^2=3(xy+xz+yz)$  $(2x-3y-3z)^2=5y^2+5z^2+30yz=5(y^2+z^2+6yz) $ So this means  $5$  divides  $y^2+z^2+6yz$  from quadratic residue  $5$  both divides  $y$  and  $z$  . $\Rightarrow$   $5$  divides  $x$ ,  $y$  and  $z$  .Contradiction .

On the second row, the number are written in descending order  $2n, 2n -1, 2n- 2, ..., n + 1$ .

stem_md: How many natural number  $n$  less than  $2015$  that is divisible by  $\lfloor\sqrt[3]{n}\rfloor$  ?
solution_md:
$1728=12^3<2014<13^3=2197\Longrightarrow \lfloor\sqrt[3]{2014}\rfloor=12$ .

For  $n,k\in\mathbb{N}$ : $\lfloor\sqrt[3]{n}\rfloor=k\Longleftrightarrow k\le\sqrt[3]{n}<k+1\Longleftrightarrow k^3\le n\le k^3+3k^2+3k$ .
The set  $\{k^3,k^3+1,k^3+2\dots,k^3+3k^2+3k\}$  contains the multiplies of  $k$ : $k\cdot k^2;k\cdot(k^2+1);k\cdot(k^2+2);\dots;k\cdot(k^2+3k+3)$ , hence  $3k+4$  numbers divisible by  $k$ .

For  $k\in\mathbb{N},\;1\le k\le11$ :
The set  $[k^3,(k+1)^3)\cap\mathbb{N}$  contains  $3k+4$  numbers divisible by  $\lfloor\sqrt[3]{n}\rfloor=k$ .

For  $k=12$ :
The set  $\{1728,1729,1730,\dots,2014\}$  contains the multiplies of  $12$ : $12\cdot144,12\cdot145,12\cdot146,\dots,12\cdot167$ , hence  $24$  numbers.

Results:
the set  $\{1,2,3,\dots,2014\}$  contains  $N$  numbers  $n$  with the property  $\lfloor\sqrt[3]{n}\rfloor|n$ , where $N=\left(\sum_{k=1}^{11}(3k+4)\right)+24=3\cdot\dfrac{11\cdot12}{2}+4\cdot11+24=266$ .

stem_md:
Students in a school are arranged in an order that when you count from left to right, there will be  $n$  students in the  first row,  $n-1$  students in the second row,  $n - 2$  students in the third row,... until there is one student in the  $n$ th row. All the students face to the  first row. For example, here is an arrangement for  $n = 5$ , where each  $*$  represents one student: $*$  $* *$  $* * *$  $* * * *$  $* * * * *$  ( first row)

Each student will pick one of two following statement (except the student standing at the beginning of the row):
i) The guy before me is telling the truth, while the guy standing next to him on the left is lying.
ii) The guy before me is lying, while the guy standing next to him on the left is telling the truth.

For  $n = 2015$ ,  find the maximum number of students telling the truth. 
(A student is lying if what he said is not true. Otherwise, he is telling the truth.)

stem_md: Given a set  $S \subset R^+$ ,  $S \ne \emptyset$  such that for all  $a, b, c \in S$  (not necessarily distinct) then  $a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc$  is rational number. Prove that for all  $a, b \in S$  then  $\frac{a - b}{a + b}$  is also rational.
solution_md:
Let  $a,b \in S$  and assume wlog that  $a \not= b$ .
We know that   $$ u = 2a^3+b^3-3a^2b \in \mathbb{Q}, \quad v = a^3+2b^3-3ab^2 \in \mathbb{Q}. $$  Hence,  $$ u+v = 3(a^3+b^3-a^2b-ab^2) = 3( a+b)(a-b)^2 \in \mathbb{Q} $$  and  $$ u-v = a^3-3a^2b+3ab^2-b^3 = (a-b)^3 \in \mathbb{Q}. $$  This implies  $\frac{a-b}{a+b} = \frac{3(u-v)}{u+v} \in \mathbb{Q}$ .

stem_md: We call the *tribi* of a positive integer  $k$  (denoted  $T(k)$ ) the number of all pairs  $11$   in the binary representation of  $k$ . e.g   $$ T(1)=T(2)=0,\, T(3)=1, \,T(4)=T(5)=0,\,T(6)=1,\,T(7)=2. $$  Calculate  $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^{2^n}T(K)$ .
solution_md:
$S_n=\sum_{k=1}^{2^n}T(K)=\sum_{k=0}^{2^n-1}T(K)$  since  $T(0)=T(2^n)=0$ . $S_{n+1}$  is formed by taking  $T(0), T(1), T(2)... T(2^n-1)$  and adding  $2^n$  to each of the inputs, which is the same as adding a  $1$  to the beginning of the  $n$ -digit number (that is, given leading zeros are not taken off). For half of these  $k$ , where the first digit of n-digit  $k$  in binary is  $1$ ,  $T(k+2^n)=T(k)+1$ . Otherwise  $T(k+2^n)=T(k)$ . So  $S_{n+1}=2S_{n}+2^{n-1}$ . Thus  $S_{n+2}=2S_{n+1}+2^{n}$  and  $2S_{n+1}=4S_{n}+2^{n}$ . It follows that  $S_{n+2}=4S_{n+1}-4S_n$ .

So  $S_{n+2}=4S_{n+1}-4S_n$ ,  $S_1=0$ ,  $S_2=1$ . 
We claim for all  $n \geq 2$ ,  $S_n=2^{n-2}(n-1)$ . Proof by induction: Base cases with  $S=2$  and  $S=3$  hold. Now assume  $S_{n}=2^{n-2}(n-1)$  and  $S_{n+1}=2^{n-1}n$ . Thus  $S_{n+2}=4(2^{n-1})n-4(2^{n-2})(n-1)=2^{n+1}n+2^{n}-2^{n}n=2^n(n+1)$  and result is proved.

So  $S_1=0$ , and for  $n>1$ ,  $S_n=2^{n-2}(n-1)$ .

Given a positive integer  $k$ . Prove that there are infinitely many positive integers  $n$  satisfy the following conditions at the same time:
a)  $n$   has at least  $k$  distinct prime divisors
b) All prime divisors other than  $3$  of  $n$  have the form  $4t+1$ , with  $t$  some positive integer.
c)  $n | 2^{\sigma(n)}-1$ Here  $\sigma(n)$   demotes the sum of the positive integer divisors of  $n$ .
solution_md:
Given a positive integer $k$ . Prove that there are infinitely many positive integers $n$ satisfy the following conditions at the same time: a) $n$ has at least $k$ distinct prime divisors b) All prime divisors other than $3$ of $n$ have the form $4t+1$ , with $t$ some positive integer. c) $n | 2^{\sigma(n)}-1$ Here $\sigma(n)$ demotes the sum of the positive integer divisors of $n$ .
My solution**Familiar result:** If $(a,b)=1$ then $\sigma (ab)=\sigma (a).\sigma (b)$ Back to the problem: We just care about properties $b)$ and $c)$ . If we can create a sequence $(u_n)$ has properties: the number of prime diviors of $u_{n+1}$ equal to the number of prime diviors of $u_n$ plus $1$ , then we are done (Becase $u_k,u_{k+1},...$ satisfied) $15$ satisfied because $\sigma (15)=24\Rightarrow 2^{\sigma (15)}-1\vdots 15$ According to Zsingmondy, exist a prime $q:$ $ord_q(2)=24 $ (Here it is $241$ ) We have $q \equiv 1 \,(\textrm{mod 4})$ (because $ord_q(2)=24 \Rightarrow q-1 \vdots 24 $ ) and $(q,15)=1 \Rightarrow \sigma (15q)=\sigma (15).\sigma (q) $ So $2^{\sigma (15q)}-1=2^{\sigma (15)\sigma (q)}-1 \vdots 2^{\sigma (15)}-1\vdots 15q$ $\Rightarrow 15q$ satisfied Do this $k,k+1,....$ times, we get a increase sequence as the form $15.q.p_1.p_2....$ which has more than $k$ prime divisors and all prime divisors bigger than $3$ of it are in the form $4t+1$ Q.E.D

stem_md:
Anna and Berta play a game in which they take turns in removing marbles from a table. Anna takes the first turn. When at the beginning of the turn there are  $n\geq 1$  marbles on the table, then the player whose turn it is removes  $k$  marbles, where  $k\geq 1$  either is an even number with  $k\leq \frac{n}{2}$  or an odd number with  $\frac{n}{2}\leq k\leq n$ . A player win the game if she removes the last marble from the table.
Determine the smallest number  $N\geq 100000$  such that Berta can enforce a victory if there are exactly  $N$  marbles on the tale in the beginning.
solution_md: If there is an odd number of marbles on the table, Anna wins since she can take all of them. Suppose that there is an even number of marbles on the table. The first player who takes an odd number of marbles loses since this leaves an odd number of marbles and afterwards the other player can take the rest of the marbles. So we can assume that  $k$  always is an even number less than or equal to  $n/2$ . If the number of marbles on the table is of the form  $2^m-2$  for some  $m\geq 2$  then since  $k$  is even,  $k\leq 2^{m-1}-2$ . Thus in next turn the number of marbles is  $2^m-2-k$  and since   $$ 2^{m-1}-2<2^m-2-k<2^m-2 $$   in the next turn the number of marbles is not of the form  $2^m-2$  for some  $m\geq 2$ . On the other hand assume that  $2^m-2<n<2^{m+1}-2$  for some  $m\geq 2$ . Since  $n$  is even,  $n\leq 2^{m+1}-4$  and thus  $n/2\leq 2^m-2$ . The one playing can therefore remove  $n-(2^m-2)$  marbles and leave  $2^m-2$  marbles on the table. This shows that if the number of marbles on the table is on the form  $2^m-2$ , the one not to take turn can always gurantee that the number of marbles has this form when the other player has to take turn. Therefore at some point the number of marbles will be  $2$  and the player to take turn loses the game. Thus Berta can win if and only if  $2^m-2$  for some  $m\geq 2$ , and the answer is  $2^{17}-2=131070$

stem_md:
Determine all polynomial  $P(x)\in \mathbb{R}[x]$  satisfying the following two conditions:
(a)  $P(2017)=2016$  and
(b)  $(P(x)+1)^2=P(x^2+1)$  for all real number  $x$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>great</summary>well trivially  $2016$  and  $2017$  really don't play a significant role here so we go for this :  $P(n)=n-1$  for some  $n \in \mathbb{R}$  so we have  $P(x)=(x-n)Q(x)+x-1$  for some  $Q(x)\in \mathbb{R}[x] \qquad \qquad (\spadesuit)$  

now we have  $(P(x)+1)^2=(x-n)^2\cdot Q^2(x)+x^2+2(x-n)Q(x)$   $P(x^2+1)=(x^2+1-n)(Q(x^2+1))+x^2 \qquad \qquad (\diamond)$ as we have  $(P(x)+1)^2=P(x^2+1)$  for all real  $x$  we get: $(x^2+1-n)Q(x^2+1)=(x-n)Q(x)((x-n)Q(x)+2)$ clearly  $Q(n^2+1)=0 \qquad \qquad (\clubsuit)$ so plugging  $(\clubsuit)$  in  $(\diamond)$  we get  $P(n^2+1)=n^2 \qquad \qquad (\heartsuit)$ so from  $(\heartsuit)$  we get: $P(x)=(x-(n^2+1))J(x)+x-1$  for some  $J(x) \in \mathbb{R}[x] \implies P(x)=(x-i)J(x)+x-1$  for  $i=n^2+1$ which is similar as  $(\spadesuit)$  

so clearly we continue like this to get that  $Q(x)$  has infinite degree but clearly this is not possible hence  $Q(x) \equiv 0$  

plugging this in  $(\spadesuit)$  to get: $\boxed{P(x)=x-1} \hspace{1cm} \blacksquare$</details>

solution_md: Consider any  $7$  people and pick  $6$  of them which form this cycle  $(u_{1},u_{2},...u_{6})$ . However note that if anyone of them has degree at least  $4$  we are done since he can interfere inbetween a consecutive couple of vertices in  the cycle in which he does not participate. Thus assume for the sake of contradiction that  $deg(u_{i})=3$  then  $2 | 3\cdot 7$ , contradiction. Hence, the claim is true.

Real numbers  $x,y,z$  are chosen such  that   $$ \frac{1}{|x^2+2yz|} ,\frac{1}{|y^2+2zx|} ,\frac{1}{|x^2+2xy|}  $$   
are lengths of a non-degenerate triangle .
Find all possible values of  $xy+yz+zx$  .

*Proposed by Michael Rolínek*
solution_md:
Above solution works only when  $a \neq 0$  , if  $a=0$  the first fraction would be  $\frac{1}{|a|}$  wich is absurd.

Assume that   $xy+yz+zx=0$  and  $2$  of  $x,y,z$  are equal , say  $x=y$  ,then we would have  $|x^2+2zx|=|xy+xy+zx|=0 $  wich is again absurd.

So W.L.O.G  $x>y>z$  , two of them are positive , or two of them are negative , say  $x,y$  then  $z^2+2xy$  is positive.
On the other hand  $x^2+2yz+y^2+2zx=(x-y)^2>0$  so, one of  $x^2+2yz$  or  $ y^2+2xz$  is positive .
The sum of the three fractions without absolute values would be  $$ \sum_{cyc} \frac{1}{x^2+2yz}=\sum_{ cyc}  \frac{1}{(x-y)(x-z)}=0 $$  A contradiction ,because we would have that sum of two of the fractions with positive denominators is equal to the other fraction , but  they form a degenrate triangle .

So the answer is all reals without  $0$  .

In  $\triangle ABC$  ,let  $D$  be the intersection of angle bisector of  $\angle BAC$  and  $BC$  .
Let  $E,F$  be the circumcenters of  $\triangle ABD, \triangle ACD$  ,respectively.
What is the size of  $\angle BAC$  if the circumcenter of  $\triangle AEF$  lies on the line  $BC$  .

*Proposed by Patrik Bak*
solution_md:
The answer is   $\angle{BAC}=120$ Let  $O=$  the circumcenter of  $\triangle{ABC}$  ;  $G=$  the circumcenter of  $\triangle{AEF}$  $OE\perp AB$  and  $OF\perp AC$  thus  $\angle{EOF}=180-\angle{BAC}$ ,but  $\angle{EAF}=\angle{BAC}$   (angle chasing) Therefore  $A,E,F,O$  are on a circle
Moreover : $\angle{EAD}=\angle{FAD}=\mid B-C\mid$  so  $OE=OF$   $EF\perp AD$  ;  $GO\perp EF$  so  $GO\parallel AD$   $(1)$  $G$  is on the perpendicular bisector of  $AO$   $(2)$  $G\in BC$   $(3)$ From  $(1)+(2)+(3)$  using complex numbers with  $A=a^2,B=b^2,C=c^2$  we get  $b^2+c^2-bc=0 \iff \angle{BAC}=120 $

solution_md:
The system of Diophantine equations $(1) \;\; a + b = cd$ , $(2) \;\; c + d = ab$ is given.

We.may WLOG assume  $a \leq b, c \leq d$  and  $a \leq c$ .  Combining equations (1) and (2) we obtain $(a + b)(c + d) = abcd$ ,

yielding ${\textstyle (3) \;\; (\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b})(\frac{1}{c} + \frac{1}{d}) = 1}$ .

If  $2 \leq a = \min\{a,b,c,d\}$ , then  ${\textstyle \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} \geq 1}$  and  ${\textstyle \frac{1}{c} + \frac{1}{d} \geq 1}$  with equality iff  $a=b=c=d=2$ .  
Finale assume   $a=1$ .  Consequently by equations (1)-(2) we obtain $b = cd - 1 = c + d$ ,

i.e. $(c - 1)(d - 1) = 2$ ,

which implies  $(c,d)=(2,3)$  (since  $b \leq c$ ) and  $b = cd - 1 = 2 \cdot 3 - 1 = 6 - 1 = 5$ .**Conclusion:**. The only solutions of the system of equations (1)-(2) in natural natural numbers are $(a,b,c,d) = (2,2,2,2), (1,5,2,3), (1,5,3,2), (5,1,2,3), (5,1,3,2), (2,3,1,5), (2,3,5,1), (3,2,1,5), (3,2,,5,1)$ .

\frac{DA}{DB} \cdot \frac{EA}{EB} = \left( \frac{CA}{CB} \right)^2.
\]

Indeed,
\[
\frac{DA}{DB} \cdot \frac{EA}{EB}
= \frac{[ACD]}{[BCD]} \cdot \frac{[ACE]}{[BCE]}
= \frac{\tfrac{1}{2} \, AC \cdot DC \cdot \sin(\angle ACD)}
{\tfrac{1}{2} \, BC \cdot DC \cdot \sin(\angle BCD)}
\cdot
\frac{\tfrac{1}{2} \, AC \cdot EC \cdot \sin(\angle ACE)}
{\tfrac{1}{2} \, BC \cdot EC \cdot \sin(\angle BCE)}.
\]

Since  $\angle ACD = \angle BCE$ , it follows that  $\angle ACE = \angle BCD$ . Hence,
\[
\frac{DA}{DB} \cdot \frac{EA}{EB}
= \frac{AC}{BC} \cdot \frac{AC}{BC}
= \left( \frac{AC}{BC} \right)^2.
\]

Returning to the problem, we have  $BC = 3$ ,  $CA = 2$ ,  $AB = 4$ , and  $AD = 1$ , so  $BD = 3$ .

Applying the above result, we get
\[
\frac{EA}{EB} \cdot \frac{1}{3} = \left( \frac{2}{3} \right)^2
\quad \Rightarrow \quad
\frac{EA}{EB} = \frac{4}{3}.
\]

Also, since  $EA + EB = AB = 4$ , it follows that
\[
EB = \frac{12}{7}.
\]

stem_md: Find the number of unordered triples of distinct positive integers such that their product are exactly  $12$  times their sum. (Hence, for example,  $(3, 6, 18)$  and  $(3, 18, 6)$  are considered as a same triple. )
solution_md:
Let's suppose  $1\le a\le b\le c$  and we have  $abc=12(a+b+c)\iff a^2bc=12(a^2+ab+ac)\iff (ab-12)(ac-12)=12(a^2+12)$ .
If both factors on LHS are negative then  $|ab-12|,|ac-12|<12$ , contradiction. Hence both factors are positive.
If  $a\ge 4$  then  $(a^2-12)^2\le (ab-12)(ac-12)=12(a^2+12)\iff a^4-24a^2\le 12a^2\iff a\le 6$ .
Hence we always have  $a\le 6$ .  For each  $1\le a\le 6$  we can check the factorisation above.
For  $a=1$  we have  $(b-12)(c-12)=12\cdot 13=2^2\cdot 3\cdot 13$  which gives 6 solutions.
For  $a=2$  we have  $(b-6)(c-6)=48$  and 5 solutions.
For  $a=3$  we have  $(b-4)(c-4)=28$  and 3 solutions.
For  $a=4$  we have  $(b-3)(c-3)=21$  and 2 solutions.
For  $a=5$  we have   $(5b-12)(5c-12)=324$  and  $(5b-12,5c-12)=(3,108),(18,18)$ .
For  $a=6$  we have  $(b-c)(c-2)=16$  and 3 solutions.

stem_md: Let \(ABC\) be an acute triangle with circumcircle \(\mathcal{C}\) and incenter \(I\). Let \(\mathcal{C}_1\) be the circle tangent to \(AB\), \(AC\), and \(\mathcal{C}\) inside \(\mathcal{C}\), and \(T\) the intersection point between \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{C}_1\). Let \(E\) and \(F\) be the feet of the angle bisectors of \(\angle ABC\) and \(\angle ACB\), respectively. Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be the intersection points of \(EF\) with \(\mathcal{C}\). Let \(J\) be the reflection of \(I\) over \(EF\) and \(\mathcal{C}_2\) the circumcircle of \(JXY\). Let \(L\) be the intersection point of the common tangents of \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{C}_2\). Prove that \(L\), \(J\), and \(T\) are collinear.
solution_md:
Basically let  $BI, CI$  hit  $(ABC)$  at  $M_B, M_C$  respectively and let  $N$  midpoint of arc  $BAC$ , then from  $\sqrt{bc}$  invert we trivially have  $T,I,N$  colinear and now from degen Pascal and antiparallels we have that the tangent from  $A$  to  $(ABC)$ , parallel from  $I$  to  $BC$  and  $EF$  are concurrent at a point  $Z$ , however projecting from  $I$  we get that  $AM_CTM_B$  is harmonic so  $TZ$  is also tangent to  $(ABC)$ .
Now notice this implies that  $(AJIT)$  is the apollonius circle of  $\triangle XTY$  so in fact from the tangents we have that there exists a circle through  $T,J$  tangent to  $(ABC)$  and the reflection of  $(XIY)$  over  $EF$  and now we finish by Monge d'Alembert thus we are done :cool:.

stem_md:
For \( n \geq 2 \), an \( n \)-omino is a figure without holes formed by \( n \) unit squares such that each unit square shares an edge with at least one other square. We say two \( n \)-ominoes are identical if they have the same shape when rotated or if they are the reflection of one of the other.
(In the image we can see the 5 different 4-ominoes)
 Determine all integers \( n \geq 2 \) such that we can partitionate an \( n \times n \) board with pairwise distinct \( n \)-ominoes.

**Attachments:**

![Captura de pantalla 2025-07-25 182239.png](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/f/e/188e193001539a4afc9a2e212c20b620ff66f1.png)
solution_md:
For  $n=2,3$  there aren't enough  $n$ -ominoes. For  $n=4$  let us label the  $4$ -ominoes O, L, T, S, I respectively. T is the only  $4$ -ominoe with an unequal number of white and black squares on a checkerboard tiling, so it can't be used since a  $4\times 4$  square has an equal number of white and black squares. The I has to be used on the edge, leaving us the O, L and S to cover a  $3\times 4$  rectangle but this is impossible since any placement of O leaves an area which cannot be tiled by a L and an S, so  $n=4$  also fails.

For  $n=5$  we have the following placement using the standard pentamino notation: I-pentamino is placed at the edge, and in the remaining  $4\times 5$  rectangle we place in three corners L, V and Y pentaminoes and a P pentamino in the remaining space.

For  $n>5$  we will divide the board into  $3\times n$  strips. For  $n=3k+1$  we will add a  $1\times n$  n-omino and for  $n=3k+2$  we will add one  $1\times n$  n-omino and a  $1\times (n-1)+1$  L-shaped n-omino, swapping the corner squares with one  $3\times n$  strip. 

For each  $3\times n$  stripes, let  $k$  and  $l$  be non-negative numbers such that  $k+l
\leq n-3$  and  $k\geq l, n-3-k-l$ . The left edge  $3\times 1$  column is given to the middle  $n$ -omino, and then the next  $l$  in the top row,  $k$  in the middle row and  $n-3-k-l$  in the bottom row. Then the remaining  $n-k-1$  fields in the middle row are redistributed between the top and bottom  $n$ -omino with  $l+1$  going to the top  $n$ -omino and the rest to the bottom one. The number of unique choices and combinations we can use for a stripe is far larger than  $n/3$  for  $n>8$ . For the swap operation we select a stripe where the two rightmost squares in the middle are given to the top  $n$ -omino so it remains connected after it loses the corner square and an extra square in the top row is given to this  $n$ -omino from the middle  $n$ -omino, which gets an extra square from the swap.

The only cases which warrant special attention are  $n=6,7,8$ . For  $n=6$  and  $n=7$  we can select  $k=n-3$ ,  $l=0$  for the first stipe, splitting the two middle fields between the top and bottom, and  $k=n-5$ ,  $l=1$  for the second stripe, giving the middle two of the remaining  $4$  squares in the middle row to the top  $n$ -omino and the rest to the bottom  $n$ -omino.

For  $n=8$ , as with all numbers of the form  $3k+2$ , we must be careful to ensure that no  $n$ -omino in the stripes is equal to the  $1\times (n-1)+1$  L-shaped n-omino. We construct the first stripe in the same way as the second stripe for the cases  $n=6, 7$ . For the second stripe, the one that will be used for the swap, we select  $k=3$ ,  $l=2$  and give the rightmost two of the squares in the middle row to the top  $n$ -omino and the remaining one to the bottom  $n$ -ominoe.

Thus the answer to the problem is  $n\geq 5$ .

stem_md:
Consider the system of equations:
    \[
    \begin{cases} 
    b^2 + 1 = ac,  
    c^2 + 1 = bd, 
    \end{cases}
    \qquad (1)
    \]
    where \( a, b, c, d \) are positive integers.**a)** Prove that there are infinitely many positive integer solutions to system (1).**b)** Prove that if \((a, b, c, d)\) is a solution of (1), then
        \[
        a = 3b - c, \quad d = 3c - b.
        \]
solution_md:
A classic vieta jumping problem states that if  $xy$  divides  $x^2 + y^2 + 1$  then  $x^2 + y^2 + 1 = 3xy$ .
By the same method you can generate infinitely many solutions  $(x,y)$  to that equation. So then  $(a,b,c,d) = (3x-y ,x, y, 3y-x)$  is a solution and there are infinitely many of them.
For the  $(b)$  part we can check that:  $$ ad = (\frac{b^2+1}{c})(\frac{c^2+1}{b}) = bc + \frac{b^2 + c^2 + 1}{bc} $$  So the latter expression is an integer, then  $b^2 + c^2 + 1 = 3bc$  where we get  $a = 3b - c$  and  $d = 3c - b$ .

$\mathfrak{The \; Thirtieth\; of\; July,\; 2025}$  ʕ•ᴥ•ʔ
<details><summary>Solution - grinding problems</summary>$$ \color{red} \spadesuit\color{red} \boxed{\textbf{Solution.}}\color{red} \spadesuit $$  We notice that:  $$ x^2+y^2+z^2=(x+y+z)^2-2(x y+y z+z x)=25-2(x y+y z+z x) $$  so to minimize  $x^2+y^2+z^2$ , we must maximize  $x y+y z+z x$ .

Hence:  $$ x y+y z+z x \leq 8, \quad x y+y z+z x \geq \frac{125}{16} $$  so  $$ x^2+y^2+z^2 \geq 25-2 \cdot 8=9 $$  Equality achieved when  $x=1, y=z=2$ , as it satisfies:  $$ x+y+z=5, \quad \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{z}=1+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=2 $$</details>

stem_md:
Let  $k$  be an odd integer greater than  $1$ . On a table there are  $k$  piles of stones: the first has  $1$  stone, the next has  $2$  stones, the next has  $3$  stones, and so on until the last one, which has  $k$  stones. In the first step,  $3$  piles are chosen and all their stones are combined into a new pile, from which  $1$  stone is removed. In the second step,  $3$  piles are chosen and all their stones are combined into a new pile, from which  $2$  stones are removed. In general, in step  $n$ ,  $3$  piles are chosen and all their stones are combined into a new pile, from which  $n$  stones are removed. After several steps, only a single pile remains on the table, containing  $p$  stones.
[list=a]
[*]Prove that  $p$  is a perfect square if and only if the numbers  $2k+2$  and  $3k+1$  are perfect squares.
[*]Find the minimum value of  $k$  for which  $p$  is a perfect square.
[/list]**Note:** In each step, the stones that are removed are discarded permanently.
solution_md: *Kinda annoying...* :maybe: Notice, that the total number of steps is $\frac{k - 1}{2}$ , consequently the total number of stones at the end is invariantly given by, \[ \frac{k(k + 1)}{2} - \frac{\frac{k - 1}{2} \cdot \left( \frac{k - 1}{2} + 1 \right)}{2} = \frac{k^2 + k - \frac{k^2 - 2k + 1}{4} - \frac{k - 1}{2}}{2} = \frac{8k^2 + 8k - 2k^2 + 4k - 2 - 4k + 4}{16} = \frac{6k^2 + 8k + 2}{16} \] now notice that $6k^2 + 8k + 2 = (2k + 2)(3k + 1)$ , and by Euclid's Algorithm we know that $(2k + 2, 3k + 1) = (2k + 2, k - 1) = (4, k - 1)$ , if this expression is $4$ or $1$ then both terms are squares themselves. Thus, we only need to consider the case when $(2k + 2, 3k + 1) = 2$ , then let $2k + 2 = 2(k + 1) = 2x^2$ and let $3k + 1 = 2y^2$ then we know that, \[ 3x^2 - 2y^2 = 3k + 3 - 3k - 1 = 2 \] however now notice that modulo $3$ this implies that \[ -2y^2 \equiv 2 \pmod{3} \implies y^2 \equiv -1 \equiv 2 \pmod{3} \] which is impossible modulo $3$ . Consequently both $2k + 2$ and $3k + 1$ are squares. $\blacksquare$ *Note:* It is simple to check that $k = 161$ gives $2k + 2 = 18^2$ and $3k + 1 = 22^2$ .

stem_md: Let  $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{100}$  and  $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_{100}$  be  $200$  distinct real numbers. On a  $100\times 100$  board, the number  $a_i + b_j$  is written in the cell of row  $i$  and column  $j$ . It turns out that in each column, the product of the  $100$  numbers is equal to  $1$ . Prove that in each row, the product of the  $100$  numbers is equal to  $-1$ .
solution_md: Let  $P(x) = (x+a_1)(x+a_2)\cdots (x+a_{100})$ . By the problem statement for each  $j$ ,   $$ \prod_{1 \leqslant i \leqslant 100} (a_i + b_j) = 1 $$  That is   $$ P(b_j) -1 = 0 $$   for all  $1 \leqslant j \leqslant 100$ . Hence, the polynomial  $Q(x) = P(x) -1$  has roots  $b_1,b_2,\dots, b_{100}$ . Thus, we have   $$ P(x) -1= Q(x) = \prod_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant 100} (x-b_j) $$  Substituting  $x$  with  $-a_i$  gives   $$ -1 = \prod_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant 100} (a_i +b_j) $$   which is exactly the product of the number in each row.

stem_md: On the real line,  $22$  points are marked:  $$ 0 \leqslant a_1 < a_2 < a_3 < \cdots < a_{21} < a_{22} \leqslant 1. $$  The allowed operation is to choose any two points  $A$  and  $B$ , erase them, and mark the midpoint of  $AB$ . Prove that, regardless of the initial configuration of the  $22$  points, it is possible to perform  $20$  allowed operations so that, after these operations, the distance between the only two remaining points is at most  $0.001$ .**Note:** Assume that in each operation, the midpoint of  $AB$  does not coincide with any of the already marked points.
solution_md:
<details><summary>A simple solution</summary>Let us consider the eleven differences   $\ a_2-a_1$ ,   $a_4-a_3$ , ...,   $a_{22}-a_{21}$   arranged in the non-increasing order and name them  $b_j$ 's according to this order: 
\[
b_1 \geqslant b_2 \geqslant b_3 \geqslant ... \geqslant b_{11}\ , \ \ \ \ \sum_{j=1}^{11}b_j\le 1\ .
\]

Now we will prove that if we pick two sets of  $11$  numbers: one from each pair  $(a_1, a_2)$ ,  $(a_3,a_4)$ , ... ,  $(a_{21}, a_{22})$  and its complimentary set (also, one from each pair) and consecutively average each set to a single number, then the distance between the remaining two numbers will be less than  $0.001$ . 

Given any set of  $11$  numbers  $z_1, z_2, ..., z_{11}$ , the procedure of consecutive averaging produces the following number:
\[
\frac{z_1+z_2+2\cdot z_3+4\cdot z_4+\cdots + 256\cdot z_{10}+512\cdot z_{11}}{1024}\ .
\]    
Therefore, the difference of the two remaining numbers in our procedure will be 
equal
\[
\frac{\pm b_1\pm b_2 \pm 2\cdot b_3 \pm 4\cdot b_4\pm \cdots \pm 256\cdot b_{10}\pm 512\cdot b_{11}}{1024}\ ,
\]
where there are  $2^{11}$  choices of signs according to which number from each pair we pick for the first set and the second set. Since  $1/1024<0.001$ , we only need to show that the  $\pm$  signs can be picked in such a way that the numerator is between  $-1$  and  $1$ . 

This we will prove by induction. Moreover, we will prove a more general claim that the largest gap (the gaps are the distances between two neighbouring numbers) in all possible combinations of the  $\pm$  signs is  $\leqslant 2$ . From this it will follow that there exists a combination of signs such that the corresponding sum is within the distance of  $1$  from zero and the claim follows. 

Base of induction:  $k=1$  , where we have only two sums:  $\pm b_1$  , and the distance between them is  $2b_1\leqslant 2$ . 

Inductive assumption: all the gaps in the possible choices of  $\pm$  signs (producing the set  $S$  of  $2^k$  sums)
\[
S=\{ \pm b_1\pm b_2 \pm 2\cdot b_3 \pm 4\cdot b_4\pm \cdots \pm 2^{k-2}\cdot b_{k}\} 
\]  
are  $\leqslant 2$ . 
Now consider the two new sets:
\[
S_1=-2^{k-1}\cdot b_{k+1}+S \ \ \ \ \ \ \text{ and} 
\ \ \ \ \ \  S_2=2^{k-1}\cdot b_{k+1}+S\ .
\]
Each one of them, by inductive assumption, has all the gaps of size  $\leqslant 2$ . But this sets overlap. Indeed, both contain positive and negative numbers. For example, let us show that the set  $S_1$  contains a non-negative number: choose all signs except for the first one as  $+$ : 
\[
-2^{k-1}\cdot b_{k+1} + b_1+ b_2 + 2\cdot b_3 + 4\cdot b_4+ \cdots + 2^{k-2}\cdot b_{k} = 
\]
\[
 (b_1-b_{k+1}) + (b_2-b_{k+1}) + 2\cdot (b_3-b_{k+1}) + 4\cdot (b_4-b_{k+1})
+ \cdots + 2^{k-2}\cdot (b_{k}-b_{k+1}) \ge 0\ ,
\]
because the sequence of  $b_j$ 's is non-increasing. And therefore we are done.</details>

stem_md:
Consider a cyclic quadrangle. For each of the four triangles formed by three vertices of the quadrangle, consider its incircle. For each pair of four circles, consider the point where their external common tangents cross. Prove that these six points are collinear. (The radii of the four circles are assumed pairwise distinct.)

*Proposed by Andrei Chiriță*
solution_md:
Cute. Let  $ABCD$  be the quadrilateral with circumcircle  $\Omega$ , let  $\omega_A$  of centre  $I_A$  be inscribed in  ${}\triangle BCD$ , and define the same things for  $B$ ,  $C$  and  $D$ . Let  $P_{XY}$  be the exsimilicenter of  $\omega_X$  and  $\omega_Y$  for  $X, Y\in \{A,B,C,D\}$ .
By the Japanese theorem  $I_AI_BI_CI_D$  rectangle, let  ${}\omega$  be its circumcircle. Since by angle-chasing  $CDI_AI_B$  is cyclic, and as  $P_{AB}=I_AI_B\cap CD$ , it follows that  ${}P_{AB}$  is the radical centre of  $\omega$ ,  $\Omega$  and  $(CDI_AI_B)$ , so  $P_{AB}$  lies on the radical axis  $\ell$  of  $\omega$  and  $\Omega$ . Similarly  $P_{BC}, P_{CD}, P_{DA}\in \ell$ . But by Monge's theorem  $P_{AC}\in P_{AB}P_{BC}$  and  $P_{BD}\in P_{BC}P_{CD}$ , so the six exsimilcenters are collinear as desired.

Consider a finite number of squares whose total area (the sum of individual areas) is at most  $1/2$ . Is it possible to pack these squares in a unit square? (A packing in an arrangement with no interior overlaps.)

solution_md: <details><summary>Sketch cuz I'm lazy</summary>Just use induction on the number of squares in Polya Paradox style, using the following lemma at the induction step, which can be itself proved by a reasonably straightforward induction.**Lemma.** If  $R$  is a rectangle and  $S$  is a set of squares whose areas sum to at least half of  $R$ 's area so that  $S$  contains a square of side equal to the smaller side of  $R$ . Then we can pack some of the squares in  $S$  inside  $R$  so that at least half of its area is covered.</details>

stem_md:
For what positive integers  $n$  does there exist an integer  $k\geq 2$  such that   $$ nab \mid (a+b)^k-a^k-b^k $$   for all positive integers  $a$  and  $b$ ?

*Proposed by David Anghel*
solution_md:
Let  $P(a, b) = (a+b)^k - a^k - b^k$ . The condition is that  $nab \mid P(a, b)$  for all  $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ . This implies  $n \mid \frac{P(a, b)}{ab}$  for all  $a, b$ . $Claim$   $1:$  If such a  $k$  exists, then  $n \mid k$ . $Proof:$ Consider the polynomial expansion of  $P(a, b)$ :  $$ P(a, b) = \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} \binom{k}{i} a^i b^{k-i} = \binom{k}{1} ab^{k-1} + \binom{k}{2} a^2 b^{k-2} + \dots $$  We are given that  $nab$  divides this sum for all  $a, b$ . Let us fix  $b=1$ . Then we must have:  $$ n \mid \frac{P(a, 1)}{a} = \binom{k}{1} \cdot 1 + \binom{k}{2} a + \binom{k}{3} a^2 + \dots + \binom{k}{k-1} a^{k-2} $$    $$ n \mid k + \binom{k}{2} a + \dots + k a^{k-2} $$  Since this divisibility must hold for all positive integers  $a$ , let us choose  $a$  to be a multiple of  $n$  (e.g.,  $a=n$ ). Then every term containing  $a$  becomes divisible by  $n$ .  $$ k + \binom{k}{2} n + \dots \equiv k \pmod n $$  Thus, for the sum to be divisible by  $n$ , we must have  $n \mid k$ .  $\square$  $\blacksquare$  $Claim$   $2:$   $n$  must be square-free. $Proof:$ Suppose for the sake of contradiction that  $n$  is not square-free. Then there exists a prime  $p$  such that  $p^2 \mid n$ .
From Claim 1, we know  $n \mid k$ , which implies  $p^2 \mid k$ .
The given condition implies  $n \mid \frac{(a+b)^k - a^k - b^k}{ab}$ . Taking  $a=1, b=1$ , we get:  $$ n \mid \frac{2^k - 2}{1} \implies n \mid 2^k - 2 $$  Since  $p^2 \mid n$ , it must be that  $2^k \equiv 2 \pmod{p^2}$ .
Squaring  $2^k \equiv 2$  is not immediately contradictory, so let us look at the general condition modulo  $p^2$ .
For any integer  $x$ , choose  $a=1, b=x-1$ . The condition implies  $n \mid (1+(x-1))^k - 1^k - (x-1)^k$ , so:  $$ x^k \equiv 1 + (x-1)^k \pmod{p^2} $$  By induction (or linearity), this implies  $x^k \equiv x \pmod{p^2}$  for all integers  $x$ .
This requires  $k \equiv 1 \pmod{\phi(p^2)}$ , where  $\phi(p^2) = p(p-1)$ .
So,  $k = 1 + m \cdot p(p-1)$  for some integer  $m$ .
However, we also established  $p^2 \mid k$ .
Substituting  $k$ :  $$ 1 + m p(p-1) \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2} $$    $$ 1 - mp \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2} $$    $$ 1 \equiv 0 \pmod p $$  This is a contradiction. Therefore,  $n$  cannot have any square prime factors.  $\square$  $\blacksquare$  $Claim$   $3:$  For any prime factors  $p$  and  $q$  of  $n$ ,  $p \nmid q-1$ . $Proof:$ This is equivalent to saying  $\gcd(n, \phi(n)) = 1$ .
Let  $p$  and  $q$  be prime factors of  $n$ . From the problem statement, for any  $x$ , we must have  $nab \mid (a+b)^k - a^k - b^k$ . This implies divisibility by  $q$ .
Using a similar logic to Claim 2 (specifically  $x^k \equiv x \pmod q$ ), we require  $k \equiv 1 \pmod{q-1}$ .
From Claim 1, we know  $n \mid k$ , so  $p \mid k$ , which means  $k \equiv 0 \pmod p$ .
Now, suppose  $p \mid q-1$ .
Then  $k \equiv 1 \pmod{q-1} \implies k \equiv 1 \pmod p$ .
But we also have  $k \equiv 0 \pmod p$ .
This gives  $1 \equiv 0 \pmod p$ , a contradiction.
Thus, no prime factor  $p$  of  $n$  can divide  $q-1$  for any prime factor  $q$  of  $n$ .  $\square$  $\blacksquare$  $Claim$   $4:$  The conditions derived are sufficient. $Proof:$ We propose that any square-free integer  $n$  satisfying  $\gcd(n, \phi(n)) = 1$  is a solution.
We need to construct a  $k \ge 2$ . Consider the system of congruences:
1.  $k \equiv 0 \pmod n$ 2.  $k \equiv 1 \pmod {\phi(n)}$ Since  $\gcd(n, \phi(n)) = 1$ , by the Chinese Remainder Theorem, there exists a unique solution for  $k$  modulo  $n\phi(n)$ . Since  $n \ge 1$ , we can choose  $k > 1$ .
We check if  $nab \mid (a+b)^k - a^k - b^k$ . Since  $n$  is square-free, it suffices to show that for every prime  $p \mid n$ ,  $pab \mid (a+b)^k - a^k - b^k$ .
Since  $k \equiv 1 \pmod{\phi(n)}$  and  $(p-1) \mid \phi(n)$ , we have  $k \equiv 1 \pmod{p-1}$ .
By Fermat's Little Theorem,  $x^k \equiv x \pmod p$  for all  $x$ .
Thus,  $(a+b)^k - a^k - b^k \equiv (a+b) - a - b \equiv 0 \pmod p$ .
So  $p$  divides the expression.
To satisfy the condition  $pab \mid \dots$ , we verify:  $$ \frac{(a+b)^k - a^k - b^k}{ab} = \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} \binom{k}{i} a^{i-1} b^{k-1-i} $$  We need this sum to be divisible by  $p$ .
If  $p \nmid a$  and  $p \nmid b$ , we already know the numerator is divisible by  $p$  and the denominator is coprime to  $p$ , so the ratio is divisible by  $p$ .
If  $p \mid a$  (or similarly  $b$ ), the expansion becomes:  $$ \frac{(a+b)^k - a^k - b^k}{ab} = k b^{k-2} + \text{terms divisible by } a $$  Since  $k \equiv 0 \pmod n$ , we have  $p \mid k$ . Thus  $k b^{k-2} \equiv 0 \pmod p$ .
The expression is divisible by  $p$  in all cases.
Since this holds for all prime factors of  $n$ , and  $n$  is square-free, the condition holds.  $\square$  $\blacksquare$ The integers  $n$  are those which are square-free and for which no prime factor of  $n$  divides the totient of  $n$ . This is equivalent to:  $$ \text{All square-free integers } n \text{ such that } \gcd(n, \phi(n)) = 1 $$

stem_md:
Fix an integer  $n\geq 2$ . Determine the largest non-negative integer  $m$  satisfying the following condition: For any infinite set  $A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ , there exists a degree  $n$  polynomial with integer coefficents such that  $|A\cap f(\mathbb{Z})|\geq m$ .

*Proposed by Andrei Chiriță*
solution_md:
**Part 1. Lower Bound:  $m \ge n+1$**

We must show that for any infinite set  $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ , there exists a polynomial  $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$  of degree  $n$  such that  $|A \cap f(\mathbb{Z})| \ge n+1$ .

Let  $M = n!$ . Since  $A$  is infinite and there are finitely many residue classes modulo  $M$ , by the Pigeonhole Principle, there exists an infinite subset  $A' \subseteq A$  such that all elements of  $A'$  are congruent modulo  $M$ . That is, there exists  $r \in \{0, \dots, M-1\}$  such that:  $$ x \equiv r \pmod{n!} \quad \forall x \in A'. $$  Choose any  $n+1$  distinct elements  $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in A'$ . We will construct a polynomial  $f$  of degree at most  $n$  such that  $f(k) = a_k$  for  $k=0, \dots, n$ . Using the Newton form of the interpolating polynomial:  $$ f(x) = \sum_{j=0}^n c_j \binom{x}{j}, \quad \text{where } c_j = \Delta^j a_0. $$  **Claim 1:  $f(x)$  has integer coefficients.**
Recall the identity  $n! \binom{x}{n} \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ . More generally, for any integer  $j \ge 0$ , the polynomial  $j! \binom{x}{j} = x(x-1)\dots(x-j+1)$  has integer coefficients.
We can rewrite  $f(x)$  as:  $$ f(x) = \sum_{j=0}^n \frac{c_j}{j!} \left( j! \binom{x}{j} \right). $$  Since  $a_i \equiv r \pmod{n!}$  for all  $i$ , standard properties of finite differences imply that  $n!$  divides  $\Delta^j a_0$  for all  $j \le n$ . (Explicitly:  $\Delta^j a_0 = \sum_{i=0}^j (-1)^{j-i} \binom{j}{i} a_i$ . Since  $a_i \equiv r \pmod{n!}$ ,  $\Delta^j a_0 \equiv r \sum (-1)^{j-i}\binom{j}{i} = r(1-1)^j = 0 \pmod{n!}$  for  $j \ge 1$ ).
Thus  $c_j$  is a multiple of  $n!$ . Since  $j \le n$ ,  $c_j$  is divisible by  $j!$ . Consequently, the coefficients  $\frac{c_j}{j!}$  are integers. Therefore,  $f(x) \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ .**Claim 2: Degree of  $f$  is exactly  $n$ .**
The degree is determined by the highest term  $c_n \binom{x}{n}$ . We need  $c_n = \Delta^n a_0 \neq 0$ .  $$ c_n = \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^{n-i} \binom{n}{i} a_i = a_n + \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (-1)^{n-i} \binom{n}{i} a_i. $$  Since  $A'$  is infinite, we can simply choose  $a_n$  large enough (or distinct from the fixed value determined by  $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ ) so that the sum is non-zero.**Remark:**
Strictly speaking, in the argument above we do not choose all  $a_0,\dots,a_n$  completely arbitrarily at once.
We first fix any  $n$  distinct elements  $a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}\in A'$ .For these choices, the  $n$ -th finite difference
\[
c_n = \Delta^n a_0
= \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^{n-i} \binom{n}{i} a_i
= a_n + C,
\]
where  $C = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (-1)^{n-i} \binom{n}{i} a_i$  is a fixed integer depending only on  $a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}$ .
Hence  $c_n = 0$  can hold **for at most one value** of  $a_n$ .Since  $A'$  is infinite, we can choose  $a_n\in A'$  distinct from this exceptional value, which guarantees  $c_n \neq 0$  and thus $\deg f = n$  as claimed.


Thus, we found  $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$  of degree  $n$  passing through  $n+1$  points of  $A$ .  $$ |A \cap f(\mathbb{Z})| \ge n+1 \implies m \ge n+1. $$  **Part 2 : Upper Bound Proof**

Let \( n \ge 2 \) be a fixed integer. We will construct an infinite set \( A \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \) such that for every polynomial \( f \in \mathbb{Z}[x] \) of degree \( n \),  
\[
|A \cap f(\mathbb{Z})| \le n+1.
\]  
This shows that the constant \( m \) in the problem statement cannot exceed \( n+1 \), i.e., \( m \le n+1 \).



 **1. Suitable Sets**

A set \( S \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \) is called  **suitable**  if for every polynomial \( f \in \mathbb{Z}[x] \) of degree \( n \),  
\[
|S \cap f(\mathbb{Z})| \le n+1.
\]  
Any set with at most \( n+1 \) elements is trivially suitable.

We will construct an increasing sequence of finite suitable sets  
\[
A_0 \subset A_1 \subset A_2 \subset \cdots
\]  
and define \( A = \bigcup_{k \ge 0} A_k \). Since each \( A_k \) is finite and strictly increasing in size, \( A \) will be infinite.**2. Construction of \( A_k \) – Inductive Step**

Start with \( A_0 = \{0, 1, \dots, n\} \). This set has \( n+1 \) elements, so it is suitable.

Assume we have constructed a finite suitable set \( A_k \). Define  
\[
\mathcal{S}_k = \{\, f \in \mathbb{Z}[x] : \deg f = n \text{ and } |A_k \cap f(\mathbb{Z})| = n+1 \,\}.
\]  
These are the polynomials that **saturate** \( A_k \).**Lemma (Finiteness of Images).**
The collection of images  
\[
\mathcal{I}_k = \{\, f(\mathbb{Z}) : f \in \mathcal{S}_k \,\}
\]  
is finite.**Proof.**
Take any \( f \in \mathcal{S}_k \). There exist distinct integers \( x_0, \dots, x_n \) and distinct elements \( y_0, \dots, y_n \in A_k \) such that \( f(x_i) = y_i \) for \( i = 0, \dots, n \).  

For \( i \neq j \), since \( f \) has integer coefficients, we have \( x_i - x_j \mid f(x_i) - f(x_j) = y_i - y_j \). Let  
\[
M = \max\{\, |a-b| : a, b \in A_k \,\} \quad (< \infty).
\]  
Then \( |x_i - x_j| \le |y_i - y_j| \le M \). Thus all \( x_i \) lie in an interval of length at most \( M \).

Let \( T = \min\{ x_0, \dots, x_n \} \) and define \( t_i = x_i - T \). Then \( 0 = \min t_i \le t_i \le M \), and the \( t_i \) are distinct. Consider the translated polynomial  
\[
g(x) = f(x + T).
\]  
Then \( g \in \mathbb{Z}[x] \), \( \deg g = n \), and \( g(\mathbb{Z}) = f(\mathbb{Z}) \). Moreover, \( g(t_i) = y_i \).

Now, the \( (n+1) \)-tuple \( (t_0, \dots, t_n) \) is a choice of \( n+1 \) distinct integers from \( \{0, 1, \dots, M\} \). There are only finitely many such choices. The \( (n+1) \)-tuple \( (y_0, \dots, y_n) \) is an ordering of an \( (n+1) \)-element subset of \( A_k \), and there are only finitely many such subsets.

For each fixed choice of distinct \( t_0, \dots, t_n \in \{0,\dots,M\} \) and distinct \( y_0, \dots, y_n \in A_k \), there is at most one polynomial \( g \) of degree at most \( n \) satisfying \( g(t_i) = y_i \) for all \( i \) (by Lagrange interpolation). Hence there are only finitely many possibilities for such \( g \), and therefore only finitely many possible images \( g(\mathbb{Z}) = f(\mathbb{Z}) \). 



 **3. Choosing the Next Element**

Because \( \mathcal{I}_k \) is finite, we can choose a finite set of polynomials \( \mathcal{F}_k \subseteq \mathcal{S}_k \) such that  
\[
\{\, f(\mathbb{Z}) : f \in \mathcal{F}_k \,\} = \mathcal{I}_k.
\]  
Define  
\[
U_k = \bigcup_{f \in \mathcal{F}_k} f(\mathbb{Z}).
\]  
Each set \( f(\mathbb{Z}) \) with \( \deg f = n \ge 2 \) has natural density zero in \( \mathbb{Z} \) (because \( |f(\mathbb{Z}) \cap [-N, N]| = O(N^{1/n}) \)). A finite union of sets of density zero still has density zero, so \( U_k \) has density zero. In particular, \( \mathbb{Z} \setminus (A_k \cup U_k) \) is infinite.

Choose any integer  
\[
a_{k+1} \in \mathbb{Z} \setminus (A_k \cup U_k),
\]  
and set \( A_{k+1} = A_k \cup \{ a_{k+1} \} \).**4. \( A_{k+1} \) is Suitable**

Let \( g \in \mathbb{Z}[x] \) with \( \deg g = n \). We show \( |A_{k+1} \cap g(\mathbb{Z})| \le n+1 \).**Case 1:**\( g \notin \mathcal{S}_k \).  
  Then \( |A_k \cap g(\mathbb{Z})| \le n \). Adding at most one element \( a_{k+1} \) gives \( |A_{k+1} \cap g(\mathbb{Z})| \le n+1 \).**Case 2:** \( g \in \mathcal{S}_k \).  
  Then there exists \( f \in \mathcal{F}_k \) such that \( g(\mathbb{Z}) = f(\mathbb{Z}) \). By definition of \( \mathcal{S}_k \), we have \( |A_k \cap g(\mathbb{Z})| = n+1 \). Because \( a_{k+1} \notin U_k \) and \( f(\mathbb{Z}) \subseteq U_k \), we have \( a_{k+1} \notin g(\mathbb{Z}) \). Hence  
  \[
  |A_{k+1} \cap g(\mathbb{Z})| = |A_k \cap g(\mathbb{Z})| = n+1.
  \]

In both cases, the required inequality holds, so \( A_{k+1} \) is suitable.



 **5. The Infinite Set \( A \)**

Define  
\[
A = \bigcup_{k \ge 0} A_k.
\]  
\( A \) is infinite because each \( A_k \) is finite and strictly increasing in size.

Now let \( f \in \mathbb{Z}[x] \) be any polynomial of degree \( n \). If \( |A \cap f(\mathbb{Z})| \ge n+2 \), then there exist \( n+2 \) distinct elements in this intersection. Since they all belong to \( A \), they must appear in some finite \( A_K \) for large enough \( K \). Then \( |A_K \cap f(\mathbb{Z})| \ge n+2 \), contradicting that \( A_K \) is suitable. Therefore  
\[
|A \cap f(\mathbb{Z})| \le n+1 \quad \text{for every such } f.
\]**6. Conclusion (Upper Bound)**

We have exhibited an infinite set \( A \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \) such that no polynomial of degree \( n \) with integer coefficients can have more than \( n+1 \) common values with \( A \). Hence the largest integer \( m \) that works for  **all**  infinite sets \( A \) cannot exceed \( n+1 \), i.e.,  
\[
m \le n+1.
\]

Together with the lower bound \( m \ge n+1 \) (which is established in the first part), we conclude  
\[
\boxed{m = n+1}.
\]

stem_md: If  $n$ ,  $m$  are positive integers satisfying  $n+m=2025$ , find the maximum of  $\gcd(n, m)$ .
solution_md: The answer is  $\boxed{675}$ , achieved by  $n = 675, m=  1350$ . If  $d = \gcd(n,m)$  and  $n = xd, m = yd$ , note that  $d(x+y) = 2025$ , so  $d > 2025$  implies  $x + y < 3$ , so  $x + y = 2 \implies x = y =1$ , absurd since  $2025$  is odd.

candidates: gcd(n,m) = gcd(n, 2025-n) = gcd(n,2025) by Euclid’s algorithm. m>0 and so n<2025. gcd(n,2025) is maximized when n=2025/3 giving 675

stem_md: $n\ge 3$  is an integer.  $n$  real numbers  $a_1,a_2,…,a_n$  satisfies  $a_1+a_2+…+a_n=0$ . Prove that there is 3 different integers  $i,j,k$  such that  $3a_i^3a_j+2a_j^3a_k+a_k^3a_i\le 0$ .
solution_md: If we pick  $(u,v,w)$  uniformly at random from all possible triples, then  $\mathbb{E}[3a_u^3a_v+2a_v^3a_w+a_w^3a_u]=\frac{6}{n(n-1)} \sum_{i \neq j} a_i^3a_j=\frac{6}{n(n-1)} (\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^3 \sum_{i=1}^n a_i-\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^4) \le 0$ .

stem_md:
Find all functions  $f:N\rightarrow N$  such that  $f(m)+f(n)+mn\mid m^2f(m)+n^2f(n)+f(m)f(n)$  for all positive integers  $m,n$ .

Proposed by Gyumin Kim
solution_md:
The answer is  $f(n)=n^2$ , which clearly works since  $m^4+n^4+m^2n^2=(m^2+n^2+mn)(m^2+n^2-mn)$ .

Let  $m=n$  we get  $2f(n)+n^2 \mid 2n^2f(n)+f(n)^2$ , since  $$  0 \equiv 4(2n^2f(n)+f(n)^2)=4n^2 \cdot 2f(n)+(2f(n))^2 \equiv 4n^2(-n^2)+(-n^2)^2=-3n^4 \pmod{2f(n)+n^2},  $$  we get  $2f(n)+n^2 \mid 3n^4$ . In particular, for  $n=1$  we have  $2f(1)+1 \mid 3$ , so  $f(1)=1$ .**Claim.** For sufficient large prime  $p$ , we have  $f(p)=p^2$ .
*Proof.* First, from the discussion above,  $2f(p)+p^2 \mid 3p^4$ . If  $p \nmid f(p)$ , then  $\gcd(p,2f(p)+p^2)=1$ , so  $2f(p)+p^2 \mid 3$  which is absurd. Hence  $p \mid f(p)$ .
Let  $m=1$ ,  $n=p$ , we get  $f(p)+1+p \mid p^2f(p)+1+f(p)$ , since  $$  0 \equiv (p^2+1)f(p)+1 \equiv (p^2+1)(-p-1)+1=-p(p^2+p+1) \pmod{f(p)+p+1},  $$  we get  $f(p)+p+1 \mid p(p^2+p+1)$ . Since  $p \mid f(p)$  implies that  $\gcd(p,f(p)+p+1)=1$ , we derive  $f(p)+p+1 \mid p^2+p+1$ . In particular,  $f(p) \le p^2$ . Therefore  $2f(p)+p^2 \in (p^2,3p^2]$ , the only divisor of  $3p^4$  that lies in this interval is  $3p^2$ , so  $f(p)=p^2$ .

We now fix  $m$  and let  $n=p$ , where  $p$  is a sufficient large prime, to get  $f(m)+p^2+pm \mid m^2f(m)+p^4+p^2f(m)$ . Modulo  $f(m)+p^2+pm$ , we have
\begin{align*}
m^2f(m)+{\color{red}{p^4}}+{\color{red}{p^2}}f(m)& \equiv m^2f(m)+{\color{red}{(-f(m)-pm)^2}}+{\color{red}{(-f(m)-pm)}}f(m) 
&=m^2f(m)+f(m)^2+2pmf(m)+{\color{blue}{p^2}}m^2-f(m)^2-pmf(m) 
&\equiv m^2f(m)+f(m)^2+2pmf(m)+{\color{blue}{(-f(m)-pm)}}m^2-f(m)^2-pmf(m) 
&=pm(f(m)-m^2).
\end{align*}
Hence  $f(m)+p^2+pm \mid pm(f(m)-m^2)$ . By choosing  $p$  sufficiently large, we must have  $pm(f(m)-m^2)=0$  (because LHS grows quadratically in  $p$  while RHS grows at most linearly), hence  $f(m)=m^2$ .

stem_md:
$ABCD$  is a convex quadrilateral such that  $\angle ABC=\angle ADC=120^{\circ}$ .  $M$  is the midpoint of  $AC$ .  $X$ , $Y$  are point on ray  $MB,MD$  such that  $MX=3MB$  and  $MY=3MD$ . P is the intersection of internal angle bisector of  $\angle ABC$ , $\angle ADC$ . If  $P$  lies inside of  $ABCD$ , prove that  $\angle BPX=\angle DPY$ .

Proposed by Hyunwoo Choi
solution_md: Let  $U,V$  be two points such that  $ACU$  and  $ACV$  are equilateral triangles, with  $B,U$  on one side of  $AC$  and  $D,V$  on the other side, then  $P$  is the intersection of  $DU$  and  $BV$ . Note that  $(ABCV)$  is the Apollonian circle of  $MU$  with ratio 2, so  $BU=2BM=BX$ , and  $\angle XBV=180^\circ-\angle MBV=\angle UBV$ , so  $X$  is the reflection of  $U$  wrt  $MB$ . Similarly  $Y$  is the reflection of  $V$  wrt  $MD$ , so  $\angle BPX=\angle BPU=\angle DPV=\angle DPY$ .

stem_md: Let  $\alpha > 1$  be a positive real number. For each  $\alpha$ , determine whether or not there exist infinitely many positive integer  $n$  such that   $$ \text{lcm}\left(1,2,\cdots ,\lfloor\sqrt[\alpha]{n}\rfloor\right)\big|n $$  *Proposed by MathMaxGreat and EeEeRUT*
solution_md: <details><summary>Official Solution</summary>The answer is  $\boxed{\text{NO}}$  as expected. The idea is that  $\text{lcm}(k+1, k+2, \dots, k+m)$  is at least  $\frac{(k+1)(k+2) \cdots (k+m)}{c} = P^{m}(k)$ , where  $c = 2^{m-2}3^{m-3} \cdots (m-2)^2(m-1)$  for every positive integer  $k,m$ . (Note that this is probably the weakest bound ever for  $c$  by using product of largest possible gcd of all  $\binom{m}{2}$  pairwise distinct terms. However, it suffice to solve this problem.) Now that we fix  $m > \alpha$ . For sufficiently large  $n$ , let  $p^{\alpha} \leqslant n < (p+1)^{\alpha}$ . Since  $n$  is large, we may assume that  $p >m$ .Thus we have  $P^{m}(p-m) \mid n$ , which implies  $P^{m}(p-m) \leqslant n < (p+1)^{\alpha}$ . Which is a contradiction, since  $m > \alpha$ .</details>

In an  $n \times n$  grid,there are  $n$  cells that contain a bank, such that no  $2$  banks lie on the same row or column. Define a *bridge* with length  $k$  as a sequence of cells  $c_1, c_2, \dots, c_k$  that satisfy the following conditions  
- All  $k$  cells in the sequence are distinct.
- For each  $i = 1,2,\dots, k-1$ , the cells  $c_i, c_{i+1}$  share an edge
- Suppose that the center of  $c_i$  sits at  $(a_i, b_i)$ , then  $2$  sequence  $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_k$  and  $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_k$  are monotonous.

The government want to build multiple bridges, so that it is possible to start from any bank, then travel along adjacent cells that is in at least one bridge and reach any bank (In particular, every bank must be on at least one bridge).Moreover, any  $2$  bridges share at most  $1$  cells. However, there are costs when building bridges. Suppose there are  $T$  bridges, such that their length sums up to  $S$ , then building those  $T$  bridges costs  $S + nT$ .

Find the smallest real number  $\alpha$  such that there exist a real number  $c$  and a positive integer  $N_0$ , such that regardless of the position of  $n$  banks, the government can build bridges that costs them at most  $cn^{\alpha}$  for all  $n > N_0$ *Proposed by EeEeRUT*

}

for (int i = 1; i <= k-1; ++i) {
for (int j = 0; j <= k-2; ++j) {

}
for (int j = 0; j <= k-2; ++j) {
int t = k*j;
int u = -j+k-1-k;
int a = 0+t;
int b = k+t;
int c = 0+k+j-k+1+u;
int d = k+u;
}
[/asy]
If  $n$  is not perfect square, we construct a  $k^2 \times k^2$  in one corner with such construction, then place the rest of the banks on  $(t,t)$  with  $t = k^2 +1, k^2+2, \dots, n$ , as we will omit it in this section of proof.
First, we show that this construction always give  $O(nT) = n^{3/2}$ Consider each banks cells  $c_i$  as  $(i, \pi(i))$  if it lies on row  $i$  and column  $\pi(i)$ , where  $\pi(1), \pi(2), \dots, \pi(k^2)$  is a permutation of  $1,2,\dots, k^2$ Now,  $T$  is at least to number of monotonic subsequences  $s_1, s_2, \dots, s_T$  of  $\pi(1), \pi(2), \dots, \pi(k^2)$ , such that their union is equal to  $\pi(1), \pi(2), \dots, \pi(k^2)$ . In the diagram, one can easily see that each subsequence  $s_i$  contain at most  $k$  cells. So  $T \geqslant k$ . We have   $$ O(nT) \geqslant O(nk) \geqslant O(n (\sqrt{n} -1)) = O(n^{3/2}) $$  Now, we are left to show that we can reduce the costs to  $cn^{3/2}$ . We choice  $c=29$ . Just like before, we consider the partition of the sequence  $\pi(1), \pi(2), \dots, \pi(n)$  into  $T$  monotonous subsequences. 
By erdos, in a sequence with length  $n$ , such that  $k^2 \leqslant n \leqslant (k+1)^2 -1$  , there exist a longest  $2$  monotonous subsequences  $s_{4k}, s_{4k-1}$ , such that one is nondecreasing and one is nonincreasing, such that  $|s_{4k}|\cdot |s_{4k-1}| \geqslant n$ . Now, if we remove the subsequences  $s_{4k}, s_{4k-1}$ , the sequence  $\pi(1), \pi(2), \dots, \pi(n)$  has at most  $(k+1)^2 -1 - | s_{4k}|- | s_{4k-1}|  \leqslant (k+1)^2 - 2\sqrt{n}  = k^2$  elements. By doing this  $2$  times, the sequence of length  $n$  has  $4$  more partition and if  $k^2 \leqslant n \leqslant (k+1)^2 -1$ , then the resulting sequence after the partition has the length  $n_1$ , such that  $n_1 \leqslant k^2-1$ . Hence, applying this  $2k$  times results in the desired partition of sequence into at most  $4k$  monotonous subsequence.

Now, for any monotonous subsequence  $s_i = \pi(k_1), \pi_(k_2), \dots, \pi(k_Z)$ , we construct a bridge  $B_i$  owing to the following condition  
- Let  $c_1 = (k_1, \pi(k_1))$
- Let  $c_{g(i)} = (k_{i+1}, \pi(k_{i+1}))$ , where  $g(i) = k_{i+1} + \pi(k_{i+1}) - k_1 - \pi(k_1) +1$
- For each  $h$  between  $g(i), g(i+1)$ , construct a bridge connecting  $(k_{i+1}, \pi(k_{i+1}))$  to  $(k_{i})), \pi(k_{i+1}))$  and  $(k_{i}, \pi(k_{i+1}))$  to  $(k_{i+1}, \pi(k_{i+1}))$

This gives a bridge with length of at most  $2n$ .
Now that we have connected every bank in the same sequence, we have to connect every sequence together.
First,we choose the left most bank in each subsequence and extend a bridge that link them to the left most column on a grid, then build a bridge filling the entire column. This increase the length sum by at most  $4kn$  add at most  $1$  more bridge.
Hence the costs are at most   $$ S + nT \leqslant 2n(T-1) + (n+1)T + 4nT = 7nT + T \leqslant 28 nk + 4k \leqslant 29 n^{3/2} $$   for sufficiently large  $N$ , as desired.  $\square$</details>

stem_md:
A  $2n \times 2n$  grid ( $n>1$ ) of unit squares  is colored with four different colors; red, blue, green and pink. Each unit square is colored with one of the four given colors, and the total number of squares colored in each color must be equally  $n^2$ . Further, the union of the unit squares of the same color must form a single connected region for each four colors. A pair of adjacent unit squares is said to be in a *relationship*, if they have the same color. 

Determine the maximum number of relationships that can be formed after the coloring.

*Proposed by RL_parkgong_0106*
solution_md:
<details><summary>Official Solution</summary>The answer is  $8n^2-8n$ . **Construction:**
It is easy to prove that coloring an entire  $n \times n$  grid with one color gives  $2n^2-2n$  relationships. So coloring each quadrant of the grid with one color gives  $4(2n^2-2n)=8n^2-8n$  relationships. The following is an example of the case  $n=6$ .
[asy]
size(5.5cm);
fill((6,0)--(12,0)--(12,6)--(6,6)--cycle,pink);
fill((6,6)--(12,6)--(12,12)--(6,12)--cycle,lightblue);
fill((0,6)--(6,6)--(6,12)--(0,12)--cycle,lightred);
fill((0,0)--(6,0)--(6,6)--(0,6)--cycle,lightyellow);
for (int i=0; i<=12; ++i) { draw((0,i)--(12,i)^^(i,0)--(i,12)); }
[/asy]**Maximality:**
We first prove that every shape obtained by attaching the sides of  $n^2$  unit squares has perimeter of at least  $4n$ , assuming that this shape has no 'holes'. Let  $S$  be the shape and  $S_{\text{cover}}$  be the smallest rectangle that can cover  $S$ . Note that perimeter of  $S_{\text{cover}}$  can never exceed that of  $S$ . This can be easily shown by thinking of projecting each sides of  $S_{\text{cover}}$  to  $S$ . However, since  $S_{\text{cover}}$  covers  $S$ , their area relation will be  $S_{\text{cover}}\geq S$ . Therefore, if we set  $x, y$  as the width and height of  $S_{\text{cover}}$ , we have   $$ \text{Perimeter of  $S$ } \geq \text{Perimeter of  $S_{\text{cover}}$ }=2(x+y)\geq 4\sqrt{xy}\geq 2n $$   

Now back to the original problem...

The union of the unit squares of the same color must form a single connected region for each four colors, as the problem says. So each the union region of each color must be a shape that can be obtained by attaching the sides of  $n^2$  unit squares. As we have proved above, the shape has perimeter of at least  $4n$ . Define  $R$  as the perimeter of the union region of red unit squares, and define  $B, Y, P$  the same way.   $$ R+B+Y+P \geq 16n $$  Define  $X$  as the total length of the sides where two unit squares of different colors meet. Observe the following identity.   $$ 8n+2X=R+B+Y+P $$   View  $8n$  as the perimeter of the whole  $2n \times 2n$  grid, and think of it as adding each perimeter of the four union regions. The boundaries of the each union regions other than the perimeter of the gird are counted from  $X$ , and when counting  $X$ , the line segments included are counted twice, once from the perspective of each color, so therefore multiplied by  $2$ . Applying the above inequality gives  $X \geq 4n$ . 

Observe that  $X$  is equal to the number of segments that two unit squares of distinct colors meet.

Every two pair of adjacent unit squares are either on a relationship or two are a different color. Since there are  $8n^2-4n$  pairs of adjacent unit squares in the  $2n \times 2n$  grid, we have   $$ \text{Number of relationships}+X=8n^2-4n $$   Combining with  $X \geq 4n$  yields the wanted conclusion of maximality.</details>

stem_md:
Determine all functions  $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$  such that
\[f^n(m)+f(m+f(n))=m+f(f(m)+n) \text{ or } f^m(n)+f(n+f(m))=n+f(f(n)+m)\]for all positive integers  $m$  and  $n$ .

*Proposed by cursed_tangent1434*
solution_md: Official solutionThe answer is $f(n)=n$ for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$ only. It’s easy to see that these functions satisfy the given equation. We now show these are the only solutions. Let $P(m,n)$ be the given assertion for positive integers $m$ and $n$ Observe that from $P(n,n)$ we have, \[f^n(n)+f(n+f(n))=n+f(f(n)+n)\]which implies that $f^n(n)=n$ . In particular, $f(1)=1$ . Now, we have a key claim. **Claim :**The function $f$ is injective. *Proof :* We show that any function $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that $f^n(n)=n$ for all positive integers $n$ must be injective. Considers the arrows directed graph of $f$ . Note that if $f(a)=f(b)$ for $a \ne b$ then the loops containing $a$ and $b$ are distinct and intersect at $f(a)=f(b)$ . However, these loops are not identical (since $a \ne b$ ) and hence, they must eventually 'split'. That is, there exists some minimal integer $z$ for which $f^z(a) \ne f^z(b)$ . But then, $f(f^{z-1}(a)) \ne f(f^{z-1}(b))$ while $f^{z-1}(a)=f^{z-1}(b)$ which is a clear contradiction. Thus, $f$ must indeed be injective. There are several ways to finish from here.**Original finish via contradiction by author.**Let $\text{ord}(m)$ denote the smallest positive integer $r$ such that $f^r(m)=m$ . Clearly, $r \mid m$ . Furthermore, since \[f^{f(m)+1}(m)f^{f(m)}(f(m))=f(m)\]it follows that $\text{ord}(m) \mid f(m)$ . Now, consider $P(f(m),m)$ this gives \[f^m(f(m))+f(2f(m))=f(m)+f(f^2(m)+m) \text { or } f^{f(m)}(m)+f(m+f^2(m))=m+f(2f(m))\]since $f^m(m)=m$ we have $f^{m+1}(m)=f(m)$ and since $\text{ord}(m) \mid f(m)$ we also have $f^{f(m)}(m)=m$ . Hence, both possibilities reduce to the relation, \[f(m+f^2(m))=f(2f(m))\]which since $f$ is injective yields, $f(f(m))+m = 2f(m)$ for all positive integers $m$ . Denote this statement by $Q(m)$ . Now, say there exists some $m$ for which $f(m)=m+r$ for some $r \ne 0$ . Then, we claim the following. **Claim :** For all non-negative integers $k$ we have $f^{k+2}(m)=f(m+2^kr)=m+2^{k+1}r$ . *Proof :* Note that if $f(m)=m+r$ plugging this into $Q(m)$ we have $f^2(m)=f(m+r)=m+2r$ , confirming the base case. Now, say the result holds for some positive integer $k \ge 0$ . Then, \begin{align*} f^{k+3}(m)=f(f(m+2^kr)) &= 2f(m) - m f^{k+3}(m)=f(m+2^{k+1}r) &= 2m + 2^{k+2}r - m f^{k+3}(m)=f(m+2^{k+1}r) &= m + 2^{k+2}r \end{align*}which completes the inductive step. However, if $r \ne 0$ the integers $m+2^ir$ as $i$ ranges across the positive integers are all pairwise distinct (strictly increasing/decreasing). Thus, $f^m(m)=m$ is clearly impossible unless $r=0$ as desired.

stem_md:
Let  $\triangle ABC$  be an acute triangle with  $AB < BC <AC$ . Let  $T_A$  ( on the opposite side of  $A$  as  $BC$  ),  $T_B$  ( on the opposite side of  $B$  as  $CA$  ) and  $T_C$  ( on the opposite side of  $C$  as  $AB$  ) be points such that the angle bisector of  $\angle BAC$  and  $\angle BT_AC$  meets on  $BC$ , the angle bisector of  $\angle CBA$  and  $\angle CT_BA$  meets on  $CA$ , the angle bisector of  $\angle ACB$  and  $\angle AT_CB$  meets on  $AB$ , and
\[\angle BT_AC - \angle BAC = \angle CT_BA - \angle CBA = \angle AT_CB - \angle ACB.\]
Show that lines  $AT_A, BT_B$  and  $CT_C$  are concurrent.

*Proposed by EeEeRUT*
solution_md:
Official Solution 1First, let $S_A$ be a point outside triangle $ABC$ , such that $\angle BS_AC= 90^{\circ}$ and $BS_A = CS_A$ . Define $S_B, S_C$ similarly. [rule]**Claim 1**: $AS_A, BS_B$ and $CS_C$ are concurrent.**Proof**: Jacobi theorem. [rule]**Claim 2**: $AT_A \perp S_BS_C$ .**Proof**: Let $BS_C \cap CS_B$ at $X$ . It is easy that $AS_BS_CX$ are cyclic and its circumcenter lies on $AX$ . Let $T’_A$ be reflection of $T_A$ across $BC$ . Observe that $\triangle BT’_AC \sim \triangle S_BAS_C$ . Since, $AS_BS_CX$ is cyclic, $XBCT’_A$ is also cyclic, moreover, $A,T’_A$ and $X$ are collinear. Since, $AT’_A$ pass through the circumcenter of $AS_BS_CX$ , it suffices to show that $AT_A$ and $AT’_A$ are isogonal wrt. $\angle A$ . We apply this
lemma**Lemma**: For any quadrilateral $ABCD$ with $AB \cdot CD = AD \cdot BC$ , if there exist a point $K$ on $AC$ , $AC$ bisect $\angle AKC$ , then $A,C$ are isogonal conjugate wrt. $\triangle BKD$ .**Proof**: Let the angle bisector of $\angle ADC, \angle ABC$ meet at $I$ . Since $AB \cdot CD = AD \cdot BC$ , $I$ lies on $AC$ . Hence, it is sufficient to show that $I$ is an incenter of $\triangle BKD$ . Let $\omega$ be a circle such that its center lies on $AC$ and passes through $B,D$ . Since $ABCD$ is good, $\omega$ is apollonian circle of $AC$ with some ratio, say $\lambda$ . In the perspective of $\triangle BKD$ , $\omega$ is a circle that passes through the incenter of $\triangle BKD$ . Since $\omega$ is apollonian circle, $I$ lies on $AC$ , moreover $I$ is an intersection of $\omega$ with $AC$ . Hence, we have the lemma. $\blacksquare$ .
to $ABT_AC$ . We get the desired result. $\blacksquare$ [rule]**Claim 3**: $BS_B$ and $CS_C$ intersects on $A$ altitude of $\triangle AS_BS_C$ .**Proof**: Let the intersection point be $P$ . We apply DIT on quadrilateral $S_BS_CBC$ . There exist an involution swapping $(AP, AX), (AB, AC), (AS_B, AS_C)$ . One can easily see that this involution is isogonal wrt $\angle A$ . Hence, $AP, AX$ are isogonal pairs. Since $AX$ passes through the circumcenter of $\triangle S_BAS_C$ , $P$ lies on $A$ - altitude. $\blacksquare$ . [rule] By applying those $3$ claim, we get that $AS_A$ and $AT_A$ are both perpendicular to $S_BS_C$ , hence they are the same line. Thus, if $AS_A, BS_B$ and $CS_C$ are concurrent, then $AT_A, BT_C$ and $CT_C$ are also concurrent. Hence, we are done. $\blacksquare$

If we denote by  $\omega_A, \omega_B, \omega_C$  the Appolonius circles corresponding to the subscripted vertices, the first condition tells us  $T_A\in \omega_A$  and same for  $B,C$ . It's well-known that these circles are coaxial, and denote by  $\ell$  their radical axis. We, in fact, show that the  $3$  lines meet on  $\ell$ In fact, the following holds: **Core lemma:** If  $X\in \omega_A ,Y\in\omega_B$ , then  $AX,BY,\ell$  concur  $\iff \angle BXC - \angle BAC= \angle AYC - \angle ABC$ **Proof:** The first condition is equivalent to  $A,X,Y,B$  concyclic, or  $\angle AXB = \angle AYB$ . Letting  $D,E$  be the feet of the  $A,B$  angle bisectors, we have  $\angle AXB = \angle AXD - \angle BXD=\frac{B-C}{2}-\frac{\angle BXC}{2}$  and likewise  $\angle AYB = \frac{A-C}{2}- \frac{\angle AYC}{2}$ , from which the conclusion follows.

Now, applying the lemma to  $(X,Y)=(T_A,T_B)$  yields  $AT_A,BT_B,\ell$  concur. Similarly,  $AT_A,CT_C,\ell$  concur, so we are done

stem_md: Let  $n$  be a positive integer and   $x_1,x_2,\cdots, x_n$  be positive reals. stem_md: Let  $P_1P_2\cdots P_7$  be a regular heptagon inscribed in a unit circle. Calculate  $P_1P_2^2+P_1P_3^2+\cdots+P_1P_7^2$ .
solution_md: Let  $P_1 = 1$ , and the rest be the roots of unity. Then, it suffices to calculate \[\sum_{k=1}^6 \left|e^{2\pi ik/7}-1\right|^2 = \sum_{k=1}^6 (e^{2\pi ik/7}-1)(e^{-2\pi ik/7}-1) = \sum_{k=1}^6 -2e^{-2\pi ik/7}+2 = 14\] as required.  $\square$
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/New Post Collections/2025 NTU AMPAT/3727750.json

candidates: For any point  $X$  and regular polygon  $P_1P_2P_3\cdots P_n$  with circumcenter  $O,$  it can be proved that  $$ \sum_{k=1}^{n} (P_nX)^2 = n(r^2 + OX^2). $$  Thus the answer is simply  $7(1 + 1) = 14.$

(a) Express  $\tan \theta$  in terms of  $h$ ,  $d$ , and  $x$ .
(b) Find (with proof) the value of  $x$  that maximizes  $\theta$  in terms of  $h$  and  $d$ . Do not use calculus.
solution_md:
a) With  $\tan \alpha={{h+d}\over x}, \tan \beta=h/x$  we find  $\tan \theta=\tan(\alpha-\beta)={{(h+d)/x-h/x}\over {1+{{h+d}\over x}\cdot {h\over x}}}={{dx}\over {x^2+h(h+d)}}$ .
b) We have  $\cot \theta={1\over d}(x+{{h(h+d)}\over x})\ge {2\over d} \sqrt{h(h+d)}$  with equality when  $x=\sqrt{h(h+d)}$ .

stem_md: Find (with proof) all odd  $3\le a \le 9999$  satisfying  $10000\mid a^2-a$ .
solution_md: $$ 10000\mid a^2-a \implies 2^4 \cdot 5^4\mid a(a-1) $$  Considering tha  $a$  is odd, we have  $$ \begin{cases} 5^4\mid a 2^4 \mid a-1 \end{cases} \implies \begin{cases} a= 625l  a=16m+1 \end{cases} $$    $$ \implies 625l=16m+1 $$    $$ \implies l \equiv 1 \pmod{16} $$    $$ \implies l =16n+1 $$    $$  \implies a=625(16n+1) = 10000n+625, n\in Z $$  Given that  $3 \le a \le 9999$ , we have  $ n = 0,  a = \boxed{625}$

stem_md:
Find all triples of positive integers  $(a, b, c)$  such that 
\[ a^{20}+b^2+c^6=2026. \]
solution_md:
Since  $a^{20}<2026$ ,  $a=1$ .

Therefore,  $b^2+c^6=2025$ .

Since  $c^6<2025$ ,  $c\in\{1,2,3\}$ .

When  $c=1$ ,  $b^2=2024$ , absurd.

When  $c=2$ ,  $b^2=1961$ , absurd.

When  $c=3$ ,  $b^2=1296$ , so  $b=36$ .

Therefore, the only solution is  $\boxed{(a,b,c)=(1,36,3)}$ .
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/New Post Collections/2026 Japan Math Olympiad Preliminary/3719102.json

candidates: The answer is  $(1, 36, 3)$ . It is basically just an size issue to note that  $a=1$ , and  $c\le 3$  so brute force is not hard.

It's easy to see that since  $a^{20}, b^2, c^6$  are all positive, we must have  $a^{20} < 2026, b^2< 2026, c^6 < 2026$ , so \[ a = 1, b \le 45, c \le 3 \] 

So  $b^2 + c^6 = 2025$ . Also,  $b^2$  cannot be  $2 \pmod 3$ , so  $c^6$  cannot be  $1 \pmod 3$ , which implies  $c = 3$ . Now,  $b^2 = 2025 - 729 = 1296 \implies b = 36$ . 

So the answer is  $\boxed{(1,36,3)}$ , which clearly works.

Also, $b^2$ cannot be $2 \pmod 3$ , so $c^6$ cannot be $1 \pmod 3$ , which implies $c = 3$ . Now, $b^2 = 2025 - 729 = 1296 \implies b = 36$ . So the answer is $\boxed{(1,36,3)}$ , which clearly works.

stem_md: Find the smallest positive integer  $n$  such that  $n$  does not divide  $\lfloor \sqrt{2026}n \rfloor$ .
solution_md:
The answer is  $91$ . First we show everything else fails. Assume  $n < 91$  and  $n$  did not divide  $\lfloor \sqrt{2026} \cdot n \rfloor$ . 

Note that \[\sqrt{2026} n  - 45n = n(\sqrt{2026} - 45) < 1,\] so  $\lfloor \sqrt{2026} n \rfloor = 45n$  must be a multiple of  $n$ , a contradiction. 

Now, note that  $\lfloor \sqrt{2026} \cdot 91 \rfloor = 4096$  is not a multiple of  $91$ .

stem_md:
Find the number of triples of positive integers  $(x, y, z)$  each in the interval  $1$  to  $17$  inclusive, such that the following property holds: 

The exists a positive integer at least  $2$ , that divides all of  $xy+4$ ,  $yz+5$ ,  $zx+6$ ,  $xyz+7$ .
solution_md:
Let be  $m\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\}$  such that  $m|xy+4$ ,  $m|yz+5$ ,  $m|zx+6$ ,  $m|xyz+7$ . $\begin{cases}m|xy+4\Longrightarrow m|xyz+4zm|xyz+7\end{cases}\Longrightarrow m|4z-7\Longrightarrow 4z=k_3\cdot m+7,\;k_3\in\mathbb{N}$ .  $68\ge 4z\ge m+7\Longrightarrow m\le 61$ .
Similarly, exist  $k_1,k_2\in\mathbb{N}$  such that  $5x=k_1\cdot m+7;\;6y=k_2\cdot m+7$ . $m|xy+4\Longrightarrow m|5x\cdot 6y+120\Longrightarrow m|49+120\Longrightarrow m|169$ . $m|yz+5\Longrightarrow m|6y\cdot 4z+120\Longrightarrow m|169$ . $m|zx+6\Longrightarrow m|4z\cdot 5x+120\Longrightarrow m|169$ . $m|5x\cdot 6y\cdot 4z+840\Longrightarrow m|7^3+840=7\cdot 13^2$ .

Results the unique acceptable value  $m=13$ :  $5x=13k_1+7\Longrightarrow k_1\equiv 1\pmod{5},\;k_1\le \left\lfloor\dfrac{5\cdot17-7}{13}\right\rfloor=6\Longrightarrow$  $\Longrightarrow k_1\in\{1,6\}\Longrightarrow x\in\{4,17\}$ . $6y=13k_2+7\Longrightarrow k_2\equiv 5\pmod{6},\;k_2\le \left\lfloor\dfrac{6\cdot17-7}{13}\right\rfloor=7\Longrightarrow$  $\Longrightarrow k_2=5\Longrightarrow y=12$ . $4z=13k_3+7\Longrightarrow k_3\equiv 1\pmod{4},\;k_3\le \left\lfloor\dfrac{4\cdot17-7}{13}\right\rfloor=4\Longrightarrow$  $\Longrightarrow k_3=1\Longrightarrow z=5$ .

Hence, exist  $2$  triplets which satisfy the requested conditions:  $(x,y,z)\in\{(4,12,5);\;(17,12,5)$ .

stem_md: There is a parallelogram  $ABCD$  and a point  $E$  on  $\overline{CD}$ . Let  $M$  be the midpoint of  $\overline{AE}$ , and  $F$  the intersection of  $\overline{BM}$  and  $\overline{AD}$ . Given that  $CE=DF=3$ ,  $MB=5$ , and  $MC=4$ , find  $AB$ .
solution_md:
BM intersects CD at G.

We have  $\triangle ABM = \triangle EGM$ , so  $ABEG$  is a parallelogram.

\[
EG = AB = CD
\]

\[
DG = CE = 3 = DF
\]

Thus  $\triangle DGF$  is isosceles.

\[
\angle GBC = \angle GFD = \angle GDF
\]

Hence triangle  $BGC$  is isosceles at  $C$ .

Since  $\triangle ABM = \triangle EGM$ , point  $M$  is the midpoint of  $BG$ .

Because  $\triangle BGC$  is isosceles at  $C$ , segment  $CM$  is an altitude of triangle  $BGC$ .

\[
\Rightarrow \angle BMC = 90^\circ
\]

By the Pythagorean theorem:

\[
BC = \sqrt{CM^2 + MB^2}
= \sqrt{5^2 + 4^2}
= \sqrt{41}
\]

Since  $\triangle BGC$  is isosceles at  $C$ , we have

\[
CG = CB = \sqrt{41}
\]

Thus

\[
AB = CD = CG - DG = \sqrt{41} - 3
\]

\[
\boxed{AB = \sqrt{41} - 3}
\]

<details><summary>P22</summary>Let the circle with diameter \(IM\) be \(\omega\), and let the incircle touch \(BC,AC,AB\) at \(D,E,F\). Let \(R\) be the foot from \(D\) to \(EF\). Let \(Q\) be the sharkydevil point of \(\triangle ABC\). Notice that by incenter excenter lemma \((BIC)\) is tangent to \(PI\). Also, \((AEF)\) is also tangent to \(PI\), so by radical axes \(AQ,BC,PI\) concurr, so \(Q\) lies on line \(PA\). Also, note that as \(MQI=90^\circ\), so \(Q\) lies on  \(\omega\). Now, it is well known (proven by inversion) that \(Q,R,I\) are collinear, so by radical center theorem on \(\omega,(I),(AEF)\) we get that \(R\) lies on the radical axis between \(\omega\) and \((I)\). Note that \(-1=(E,F;R,EF\cap BC)\). Combining this with \(RD\perp EF\) we get that \(EF\) bisects angle \(BRC\). Also, note that \(\angle BER=\angle CFR\), so we get that \(\triangle BER\sim \triangle CFR\). Now, we let \(B_1,C_1\) be the projections of \(B,C\) onto \(EF\), and let \(K\) be the orthocenter of \(AEF\). By gauss bodenmiller or just radical centers we get that \(HK\) is the radical axis of the circles with diameter \(BE\) and \(CF\). We claim that \(R\) lies on the radical axis of these circles aswell. Indeed, it suffices to show \[B_1R\times RE=C_1R\times RF\]which is equivalent to showing
\[\frac{RF}{RB_1}=\frac{RE}{RC_1}\]but by the fact that \[BB_1\parallel CC_1\parallel DR\] we just need to show \[\frac{RF}{BD}=\frac{RE}{CD}\iff \frac{RF}{BF}=\frac{RE}{CE}\] but this follows from  \(\triangle BER\sim \triangle CFR\) so \(R\) lies on the radical axis of the circles with diameter \(BE\) and \(CF\), so \(H,K,R\) are collinear. Now, we claim that \(KR\perp MI\). Notice that \(MA=MI\) and \(I\) is the reflection of \(K\) over \(EF\). So we have \[\angle MIK=\angle MAK=90^\circ -\angle KIR=90^\circ -\angle RKI\]which proves the claim. To finish, note that as \(R\) lies on the desired radical axis and line \(KRH\) is perpendicular to the line through the center of the 2 circles, it has to be their radical axis as desired.</details>

By applying Pascal to the  $(A A A' T D X)$ , it suffices to show that  $DX$  and  $AA'$  intersect at the circumcenter of  $(ABC)$ . Since  $AA'$  is a diameter of  $(ABC)$ , if  $DX$  is also a diameter, we are done. Because  $AD \parallel BC$ , we have  $\angle XAD = 90^\circ$ , and therefore  $DX$  is a diameter as well.
